body.text: Myanmar’s military-backed leader Min Aung Hlaing said yesterday that his administration is reviewing the country’s relationship with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), accusing the 11-nation bloc of unfair treatment.

His comments came the day after ASEAN closed its 49th Summit and related meetings in Manila, at which the 10 other ASEAN member states decided to maintain the bar on Myanmar’s attendance at the bloc’s summits and foreign ministers’ meetings.
“They are imposing such pressure only on our country,” Min Aung Hlaing told parliament yesterday, as per Reuters’ translation of his speech.

He said that other ASEAN member states had experienced coup d’etats and political conflicts without being “singled out” in this way. “There was never pressure placed on or indignity shown toward an ASEAN member before. But with Myanmar, they are doing that,” he added.

The Southeast Asian regional bloc excluded Myanmar from its summits and foreign ministers’ meetings in late 2021 for its failure to implement the Five-Point Consensus, ASEAN’s framework for managing the post-coup crisis. Promulgated in April 2021, two months after Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup, the Consensus calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among “all parties” to the country’s conflict, and access for humanitarian aid.

During this week’s ASEAN Summit, the 10 other ASEAN members agreed to adjust their approach toward Myanmar, adopting the Thai government’s approach of “calibrated engagement” and endorsing for the first time bilateral outreach to Myanmar by individual member states. At the same time, it refused to abandon the Five-Point Consensus, saying that only after “sustained and concrete progress” in its implementation would they “consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation.”

This decision clearly came as a disappointment to Min Aung Hlaing, who, since taking office as civilian president in April, has campaigned hard for Myanmar’s full reintegration into ASEAN. He has traveled to five ASEAN member states – Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia – to generate support for its readmission to ASEAN, and formed a special committee to pursue this goal. At the same time, his administration has grown more defiant of criticisms from ASEAN member states, openly rejecting the Five-Point Consensus as an unwarranted impingement on its sovereignty and questioning the need for an ASEAN special envoy.
In his speech yesterday, Min Aung Hlaing repeated his previous comments that the ASEAN Charter requires member states to strictly respect the core principles of consultation and consensus.

“For Myanmar and ASEAN to resume normal relations, we will take into consideration Myanmar’s stance and the intentions of ASEAN member countries,” he said. He added that despite his pledge to reconsider ties with ASEAN, the new quasi-civilian administration “will continue to discuss with ASEAN member countries.”

Min Aung Hlaing’s comments inevitably raise the prospect of a scenario in which Min Aung Hlaing withdraws Myanmar from ASEAN altogether. While he did not mention that possibility, one regime propaganda account on social media explicitly flagged it as a possible option.

“The Myanmar government expects equal recognition within ASEAN in accordance with its national sovereignty,” the article stated. “Given that ASEAN membership offers little tangible benefit beyond diplomatic recognition on the international stage, Myanmar is believed to have even weighed the option of withdrawing from the bloc.”

At the same time, the account noted the increasing diplomatic normalization with Myanmar, including by the United States, and said that ASEAN “is widely expected to follow suit and resume normal engagement.”

There is no precedent for an ASEAN member state withdrawing from the bloc, and it is hard to say what impact it would have on ASEAN. Could the Myanmar military take such a drastic step? While such a possibility is hard to rule out entirely, the more likely outcome is that this is being floated by regime propagandists as a subtle threat to ASEAN rather than a realistic threat.

The reality is that despite ASEAN continuing to demand concrete progress on the Five-Point Consensus, the trends continue to move in the direction of ASEAN’s gradual normalization with Myanmar. Singapore, next year’s chair of ASEAN, is among the member states advocating a more hawkish line on Myanmar, but Min Aung Hlaing can look forward to more supportive environment when Thailand takes the chairmanship in 2028. Since the start of the year, Thailand has been the ASEAN member state most active in promoting direct talks with the coup government, and has pledged to act as a “bridge” between Myanmar and ASEAN.
